He finished runner-up at the Texas Open (now AT&T Byron Nelson) in 2016, demonstrating his ability to contend at major championship venues. 

Throughout his career, Woodland has maintained a reputation for exceptional distance off the tee, boasting a career best driving distance of 335 yards. He’s consistently ranked among the top players in terms of driving accuracy on the PGA Tour, a testament to his dedication to refining his technique. He has earned over $38 million in career earnings through 2023, with a peak season of $11.4 million in 2016. 

However, Woodland's career has also been punctuated by periods of inconsistency and health challenges. In 2019, he was diagnosed with a rare autoimmune disease called Guillain-Barré syndrome, which severely impacted his mobility and ability to swing a golf club.  He underwent extensive rehabilitation, spending over a year recovering and battling the illness. His return to competitive golf was a remarkable testament to his perseverance. He made his comeback at the 2021 Korn Ferry Tour event in Greenville, Texas, demonstrating his unwavering determination. 

In 2022, Woodland secured his second PGA Tour victory at the Corales Championship in Carlsbad, Florida, marking a triumphant return to form after his health struggles. He shot a final-round 67, adding to his 2014 victory.  As of late 2023, Woodland continues to compete on the PGA Tour, striving to recapture the form that once defined his career and showcasing the resilience and dedication that have characterized his journey as a professional golfer. He currently lives in Scottsdale, Arizona, with his wife, Melissa, and their two children.

title: James Theodore Bent
text:
James Theodore Bent, a prominent American mycologist and botanist, dedicated his life to the meticulous study of fungi, particularly those found in the Pacific Northwest. Born on August 27, 1867, in the small town of Otego, New York, Bent’s early life was steeped in a rural environment that fostered a deep appreciation for the natural world. His father, James Benton, was a Presbyterian minister, and his mother, Sarah (née Pierce) Benton, was a homemaker. He was the third of five children and displayed an early curiosity and a penchant for collecting – initially rocks and minerals, reflecting the landscape of his upstate New York home.  He received his early education at Otego Academy and later attended Hamilton College in Clinton, New York, graduating in 1889 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in natural sciences.  Despite initially intending to pursue a career in theology, a summer spent working as a forestry assistant in the White Mountains of New Hampshire solidified his interest in botany and, crucially, fungi. 

Bent’s formal training began at Cornell University in 1890, where he earned a Master of Arts degree in 1892 and a Ph.D. in botany in 1896. His doctoral dissertation, “The Flora of the White Mountains,” demonstrated his growing expertise in plant taxonomy and a methodical approach to botanical research, setting the stage for his future work. Following his doctorate, Bent accepted a position as a botanist with the United States Geological Survey (USGS) in 1897, a role that would define the majority of his career. 

His initial assignments with the USGS took him to various locations across the western United States, including Montana, Oregon, and Washington.  He began his formal mycological research in 1902, assigned to the Botany and Geology Section of the USGS in Washington D.C.  Bent’s primary focus shifted to the fungi of the Pacific Northwest, a region he would come to intimately know and document.  He recognized the vital, yet often overlooked, role fungi played in the ecosystem and began a systematic effort to classify and describe the diverse fungal species inhabiting the area. 

Bent’s most significant contribution to the field is undoubtedly the *Fungi of North America* series, a monumental undertaking that spanned nearly four decades. Beginning in 1904 and continuing until his death in 1941, he meticulously published 27 volumes of this comprehensive work. Each volume focused on a specific region of the United States, with the bulk of the series dedicated to the Pacific Northwest.  The *Fungi of North America* series contained over 12,000 named fungal species, representing an unprecedented level of detail and taxonomic accuracy for the time.  He utilized a combination of field observations, microscopic examination, and careful analysis of specimens, establishing a rigorous methodology that became the standard for mycological research. 

Beyond the *Fungi of North America*, Bent also authored numerous other scientific papers and reports for the USGS and various botanical societies. He was a prolific collector, amassing a personal collection of over 15,000 specimens, many of which are now housed in the herbarium of the United States National Museum in Washington, D.C.  He served as president of the Mycological Society of America from 1930 to 1931, further solidifying his position as a leading figure in the discipline. 

In his later years, Bent continued to work tirelessly on the *Fungi of North America*, though his health began to decline. He spent his final years in Washington, D.C., where he died on December 27, 1941, at the age of 74. His legacy is immense, not just for the sheer volume of his work, but for its scientific rigor and the enduring value of his taxonomic descriptions.  The *Fungi of North America* remains a cornerstone of mycological literature, and his meticulous approach continues to influence fungal research today.  His dedication to documenting the fungal diversity of the Pacific Northwest ensured that future generations of scientists would have a foundational resource for understanding the complex and essential role fungi play in the natural world.

title: Danny Faure
text:
Danny Faure, a prominent figure in Seychellois politics and diplomacy, was born on 22nd November 1948 in Victoria, Seychelles. His early life was deeply shaped by the island nation’s complex history, transitioning from British colony to independent republic in 1976. His father, Jean-Luc Faure, was a renowned barrister and a key figure in the Seychelles Independence Movement, and his mother, Marie-Claire Faure, was a respected teacher. Growing up in Victoria, Danny witnessed firsthand the social and political tensions that characterized the period leading up to and following independence. He received his primary and secondary education at the Victoria Junior Secondary School and the Seychelles College, respectively, demonstrating an early aptitude for academic pursuits. He then pursued his tertiary education at the University of Mauritius from 1969 to 1972, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics and Political Science.  Following this, he continued his studies at the University of Warwick in the United Kingdom, obtaining a Master of Arts degree in International Relations in 1976.

Faure’s professional career began in 1976, immediately after Seychelles gained independence. He joined the Seychelles Civil Service as a junior officer, quickly rising through the ranks due to his diligence and analytical skills. In 1979, he was appointed as a Secretary in the Ministry of Finance, a role that provided him with invaluable experience in understanding the country’s economic landscape.  He moved to the Seychelles Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) in 1982, serving as a Programme Officer before becoming the Director of Programmes in 1985. This position allowed him to develop a strong understanding of media and public communication within the Seychellois context. 

Faure’s political career began in earnest in 1986 when he was elected as a Member of the National Assembly representing the English River constituency. He served as Minister of Education in the government of James Mancham from 1991 to 1993. Following Mancham’s overthrow in a coup d'état in June 1993, Faure played a crucial role in the restoration of the government led by Sir Michel Ollivier. He was appointed Minister for Foreign Affairs in 1993, a position he held until 1996. This role significantly enhanced his international profile, allowing him to represent Seychelles on the global stage. 

In 1998, Faure was elected as the President of Seychelles, defeating Wavel Ramkalawan in a closely contested election. His presidency, spanning from 1998 to 2004, was marked by a commitment to sustainable development, poverty reduction, and strengthening Seychelles’ ties with international partners. During his tenure, he oversaw the implementation of numerous initiatives focused on environmental conservation, including the establishment of the Seychelles National Parks Authority and the expansion of marine protected areas. He also prioritized education reform, increasing access to higher education and investing in vocational training programs.  Economically, Faure’s government focused on diversifying the economy beyond tourism, encouraging the development of sectors like fisheries and renewable energy.  He strengthened Seychelles’ relationship with the European Union, securing preferential trade agreements that benefited the country's economy. 

Following the 2004 presidential election, Faure served as Minister for Finance and Economic Affairs in the government of Sir James Michel from 2008 to 2016.  He played a pivotal role in managing the country’s finances during the devastating 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, securing international aid and coordinating the reconstruction efforts.  In 2016, he was appointed as the Special Envoy for China-Seychelles relations, a role that demonstrated his continued commitment to strengthening bilateral ties with the People's Republic of China. 

Danny Faure passed away on 9th January 2023, at the age of 74, at Victoria Hospital in Seychelles, following a short illness. He is survived by his wife, Linda Faure, and their three children, Jean-Luc, Daniel, and Marie-Claire. His legacy as a dedicated public servant, diplomat, and advocate for sustainable development remains a significant part of Seychellois history.

title: Ilhan Omar
text:
Ilhan Omar was born on November 13, 1984, in Harguney, a small village in Somalia’s Hawa Sheekal District, a region known for its significant Dadaab refugee camp. Her parents, Omar Mohamud and Fauza Abdi Mohamud, fled Somalia in 1990 during the civil war, seeking refuge in the Dadaab refugee camp, specifically the Ifo and Dagahaley camps, located in Kenya. Omar spent her childhood navigating the challenges of refugee life, experiencing poverty, limited access to education, and the constant displacement inherent in the camp system. She attended a local primary school in Ifo, graduating in 2000.

The family relocated to the United States in 2001, settling in Columbus, Ohio. Omar faced significant hurdles as a young refugee adjusting to a new country. She worked multiple jobs to support her family, including as a bus cleaner and a cashier at a Walmart, while simultaneously pursuing her education. She enrolled at Howard University in 2007, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science in 2011. Following her graduation, Omar moved to Minneapolis, Minnesota, where she began working as a humanitarian aid worker for the Organization of Refugee, Immigrant and Exiled Affairs (ORIEA), a Somali community organization.

Omar’s legal career began in 2013 when she became a caseworker for the International Institute of Minnesota, an organization assisting refugees and immigrants with resettlement. She quickly excelled in her role, demonstrating a deep understanding of immigration law and a commitment to advocating for vulnerable populations. In 2017, she was admitted to the Minnesota State Bar, becoming one of the first two Somali-American lawyers in the state. She subsequently worked as a criminal defense attorney, specializing in immigrant defense, representing individuals facing deportation proceedings. 

In 2018, Omar successfully ran for the Minneapolis City Council, representing Ward 6, a predominantly Somali neighborhood. She was elected with 73% of the vote, becoming the first Somali-American and first Muslim-American woman to serve on the Minneapolis City Council. During her time on the council, she championed initiatives addressing affordable housing, community safety, and immigrant rights. She advocated for increased funding for social services, supported the establishment of a Minneapolis Office of New Americans, and worked to combat racial bias in the criminal justice system. 

In 2020, Omar mounted a bid for the U.S. House of Representatives, competing in Minnesota’s 5th congressional district. She defeated Lacy Hamilton in the Democratic primary and subsequently defeated Republican candidate Lacy Hamilton in the general election, securing a seat in the House of Representatives.  She was sworn in on January 3, 2021, becoming one of the first two Muslim-American women elected to Congress. 

As a member of the House, Omar serves on the House Judiciary Committee and the House Financial Services Committee.  She has been a vocal advocate for immigration reform, refugee rights, and social justice issues. She has introduced and co-sponsored legislation addressing issues such as border security, DACA (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals), and access to healthcare.  She has consistently spoken out against Islamophobia and anti-Semitism, sparking controversy with some of her statements, which have been criticized as anti-Semitic by some members of Congress. 

Omar's political career has not been without challenges. She faced scrutiny and accusations of misrepresenting her educational background, which she vehemently denied. She has also been the target of online harassment and threats, including numerous instances of Islamophobic and anti-Semitic abuse. Despite these challenges, she remains a dedicated public servant and a prominent voice for marginalized communities.  As of November 2023, she is currently serving her third term in the House of Representatives, continuing her advocacy for policies aligned with her values and the needs of her constituents.

title: Vicente Guerrero
text:
Vicente Guerrero Sánchez, often referred to simply as “El Libertador,” was a pivotal figure in Mexican independence and a lasting symbol of the nation’s struggle for freedom. Born into extreme poverty in 1782, his life trajectory dramatically shifted from a marginalized indigenous farmer to a celebrated military leader and, ultimately, Vice President of Mexico. He was born on February 23, 1782, in the small village of Doguita, nestled in the Sierra Norte de Oaxaca, a region then part of the Spanish Viceroyalty of New Spain. His parents, Juan Guerrero and María González, were indigenous farmers who scratched out a meager existence cultivating maize and beans on their small plot of land. Guerrero’s early life was defined by hardship; he experienced the systemic oppression and exploitation prevalent under Spanish colonial rule, witnessing firsthand the injustices inflicted upon indigenous communities and the limited opportunities afforded to those born into poverty. He received little formal education, learning primarily through observation and oral tradition.

By his early twenties, Guerrero had become a skilled muleteer, transporting goods between Oaxaca City and the port of Salina Cruz. This profession exposed him to a wider world and provided a degree of mobility, but also brought him into contact with burgeoning revolutionary sentiment. In 1810, during the initial stages of the Mexican War of Independence, Guerrero joined the forces of Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla in Oaxaca, becoming one of the first volunteers in the “Grito de Dolores,” Hidalgo’s iconic call to arms on September 16, 1810. Initially, he served as a simple soldier, fighting alongside Hidalgo’s forces in the early battles of the rebellion, including the pivotal engagement at Monte de Oro in December 1810, where Hidalgo’s army decisively defeated a Spanish cavalry charge. 

Following Hidalgo’s capture and execution in December 1811, Guerrero retreated to the mountains of Oaxaca, regrouping with other rebel leaders, most notably José María Morelos y Pavón. He quickly rose through the ranks, demonstrating remarkable military acumen and unwavering loyalty to the cause. Morelos recognized Guerrero’s tactical abilities and promoted him to General in 1816, a significant advancement considering the limited number of formally appointed officers within the insurgent army. Under Morelos's leadership, Guerrero participated in numerous successful campaigns, including the Battle of Puente de Yaón in 1817, a strategically vital victory that secured control of the main route to Mexico City. 

Morelos was captured and executed in 1815, leaving a power vacuum within the revolutionary movement. Guerrero, along with other surviving leaders, including Guadalupe Victoria and Mariano Matamoros, assumed command. He skillfully navigated the complex political landscape, maintaining a decentralized military structure and continuing the fight for independence. He spent years operating in the rugged terrain of Oaxaca and Guerrero, launching guerrilla attacks against Spanish forces and disrupting supply lines. His forces, often composed of indigenous and mestizo soldiers, numbered approximately 20,000 at its peak. 

In 1820, after years of intermittent conflict, Guerrero finally entered Mexico City, effectively ending Spanish control. He was elected Vice President of the Provisional Government, a position he held until 1829, alongside Guadalupe Victoria as President. During his tenure, he oversaw the drafting of the first Mexican Constitution in 1824, a document that enshrined principles of liberty, equality, and popular sovereignty. 

Following the ascension of Antonio López de Santa Anna to the presidency, Guerrero was forced into exile in 1829. He spent the remainder of his life in self-imposed exile in Tixtla, Guerrero, where he died on June 22, 1919, at the age of 97. He was buried in Tixtla, and his remains were later moved to Chilpancingo, Guerrero, where he is revered as a national hero. In 1972, his remains were finally transported to Mexico City and interred in the Panteón de Santa Paula, a testament to his enduring legacy as “El Libertador” – the Liberator – of Mexico.

title: Nelson Mandela
text:
Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela, born July 18, 1918, in Mvezo, a small village in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa, began his life as a Thembu royal child. His father, Gadla Henry Mphakanyiswa, was a local chief and advisor, and his mother, Nosekeni Fanny, was a midwife. Rolihlahla, a name meaning “troublemaker” in Xhosa, was given by his father, a common practice reflecting a hope for a spirited child. He was initially raised by his grandfather, Risizwe, who instilled in him a deep respect for tradition and tribal law. In 1934, Rolihlahla was sent to a Methodist school, Healdtown, where he was given the English name “Nelson.” He excelled academically and showed a natural aptitude for leadership.

In 1940, Mandela enrolled at the University of Fort Hare, South Africa’s leading institution for black Africans at the time. However, he was expelled in 1942 for participating in a student protest. This experience ignited his political awareness and led him to Johannesburg, where he worked as a mine security officer and later as a law clerk for the Witwatersrand Attorneys’ Association, a firm that employed black lawyers – a rare opportunity at the time. He completed his law degree through the University of South Africa (UNISA) in 1943, a testament to his dedication and resilience.

Mandela’s early involvement in politics began with the African National Congress (ANC) in 1944. He co-founded the ANC Youth League, advocating for a more confrontational approach to combating apartheid, the system of racial segregation and discrimination enforced by the white minority government. In 1961, he co-founded Umkhonto we Sizwe (“Spear of the Nation”), the armed wing of the ANC, which engaged in acts of sabotage against government targets. This shift to armed resistance followed decades of peaceful protests and non-violent demonstrations, which proved increasingly ineffective against the intransigence of the National Party government led by Prime Minister Daniel François Malan and later, Pieter Willem Botha.

In 1964, Mandela and several other ANC leaders were arrested and charged with sabotage and conspiracy to overthrow the government. At the Rivonia Trial, delivered a powerful speech from the dock, now famously known as his "I am prepared to die" speech, articulating his commitment to a democratic and free South Africa. He was sentenced to life imprisonment, spending the next 27 years behind bars. He was initially imprisoned on Robben Island, a notorious prison off the coast of Cape Town, where he endured harsh conditions and relentless attempts to break his spirit. He was later transferred to Pollsmoor Prison and then Victor Verster Prison.

Despite his imprisonment, Mandela remained a symbol of resistance and a focal point for the anti-apartheid movement internationally.  Pressure mounted on the South African government to release him, fueled by international sanctions, boycotts, and campaigns led by figures like American civil rights leader Reverend Desmond Tutu and British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.  In 1990, under President F.W. de Klerk, Mandela was finally released from Victor Verster Prison on February 11th.

Following his release, Mandela played a crucial role in negotiating the end of apartheid and the transition to a multiracial democracy. He worked closely with de Klerk, sharing the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with him for their efforts. In 1994, South Africa held its first multiracial elections, and Mandela was overwhelmingly elected as the country’s first black president. He served one term, from 1994 to 1999, focusing on reconciliation, social justice, and economic development. He established the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, to investigate human rights abuses committed during apartheid, offering amnesty to perpetrators who confessed their crimes.

Mandela retired from the presidency in 1999, but continued to advocate for human rights and social justice through the Nelson Mandela Foundation. He dedicated his later years to combating HIV/AIDS, promoting education, and fostering peace and understanding globally. Nelson Mandela passed away on December 5, 2013, at his home in Houghton, Johannesburg, at the age of 95, leaving behind a legacy of courage, forgiveness, and unwavering commitment to equality. His life continues to inspire generations worldwide.

title: Ayman al-Zawahiri
text:
Ayman Muhyi al-Zawahiri, born Ayman Hamza Rabia al-Hazmi on June 29, 1958, in Alexandria, Egypt, was a prominent figure in the global jihadist movement and the longtime leader of al-Qaeda. His life transitioned from a relatively ordinary upbringing to a pivotal role in shaping modern terrorist tactics and inspiring attacks across multiple continents. Al-Zawahiri’s early life offered little indication of the radical path he would later embrace. He was the son of Muhyi al-Zawahiri, a mathematics professor at Cairo University, and his mother, a teacher. He received his primary education at the Al-Azhar Islamic School in Alexandria, a prestigious institution known for its focus on traditional Islamic scholarship.  He then attended the Faculty of Commerce at Alexandria University, graduating in 1981 with a degree in business administration. 

Following university, al-Zawahiri initially worked as a clerk at a pharmaceutical company in Cairo. However, his political and ideological leanings quickly drew him towards Islamist activism. In 1984, he joined the Egyptian Islamic Jihad (EJI), a nascent extremist group advocating for the establishment of an Islamic state in Egypt.  He quickly rose through the ranks, demonstrating a keen understanding of propaganda and organizational strategy.  Al-Zawahiri’s brother, Mohammed al-Zawahiri, was a key figure within the EJI and played a significant role in introducing Ayman to the group’s broader aims. 

The EJI’s activities, including bombings and assassinations targeting government officials and security forces, led to increasing repression from the Egyptian government. In 1985, al-Zawahiri and several other EJI members were arrested following a failed assassination attempt on President Anwar Sadat, which occurred just a year prior. He spent the next seven years imprisoned in various Egyptian prisons, including Tora Prison, where he reportedly honed his skills in radical ideology and developed close relationships with other inmates, including Abdullah Azzam, a Palestinian scholar considered the “father of al-Qaeda.”  It was during this period that al-Zawahiri deeply embraced the teachings of Sayyid Qutb, a controversial 20th-century Islamist thinker whose writings promoted a radical interpretation of Islam and justified violence against perceived enemies of Islam. 

Upon his release in 1993, al-Zawahiri fled Egypt and relocated to Afghanistan, where he joined the Afghan Mujahideen fighting against the Soviet Union. He quickly gained the trust of Osama bin Laden and became his deputy, effectively managing the logistical and operational aspects of al-Qaeda.  He played a crucial role in establishing al-Qaeda’s structure, recruiting foreign fighters, and developing its operational strategies.  During this period, al-Zawahiri oversaw the planning and execution of numerous attacks, including the 1998 bombings of the United States embassies in Nairobi, Kenya, and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, which killed over 200 people. 

Following the September 11th attacks in 2001, al-Zawahiri helped al-Qaeda adapt to the international spotlight and shift its focus to targeting the United States and its allies. He was instrumental in the planning of the 2000 attack on the USS Cole in Yemen, which killed 17 American sailors.  Throughout the 2000s, al-Zawahiri continued to provide strategic guidance and operational support to al-Qaeda, contributing significantly to the group’s expansion and global reach. He frequently recorded audio messages, often delivered from Afghanistan, urging attacks against Western interests and promoting a global jihadist agenda. 

In recent years, al-Zawahiri’s role became increasingly focused on coordinating attacks in the Levant, particularly in Syria, where he worked closely with groups like Jabhat al-Nusra, al-Qaeda’s Syrian affiliate. He was killed on July 29, 2022, in a U.S. drone strike in Kabul, Afghanistan, following a decade-long hunt orchestrated by the CIA. The strike, authorized by President Joe Biden, resulted in his death alongside several other suspected al-Qaeda operatives.  His death marked a significant blow to the global jihadist movement, though the long-term impact of his leadership remains a subject of ongoing analysis.

title: Diego Suarez (garden designer)
text:
Diego Suarez, born Diego José Suarez Romero on 28 June 1935 in Santiago, Chile, was a globally recognized landscape architect whose innovative and deeply considered designs transformed public spaces across Europe and beyond. His career, spanning over five decades, was characterized by a meticulous attention to detail, a profound understanding of ecological principles, and a distinctive style that blended formal geometry with a vibrant, often exuberant, use of color and texture.  His legacy rests on a body of work that continues to inspire and demonstrate the power of landscape to enrich human experience.

Suarez’s early life provided a foundation for his future artistic pursuits. He was raised in a relatively modest household in Santiago, developing an early appreciation for the natural beauty of the Chilean landscape, particularly the coastal regions.  His father, José Romero, was a noted architect, and Diego initially followed in his footsteps, studying architecture at the Universidad de Chile from 1953 to 1958. However, he soon realized his passion lay not in building structures, but in shaping the spaces *between* them – the gardens and parks that framed and enhanced the built environment.  This shift in focus led him to pursue a degree in landscape architecture at the Universidad de Buenos Aires in Argentina from 1959 to 1963, where he was profoundly influenced by the work of landscape architects like Roberto Burle Marx, a Brazilian master whose bold, tropical designs were gaining international recognition.

Following his graduation, Suarez embarked on a period of intensive travel and study, working with various landscape architects in Europe, starting in 1963. He spent time in Italy, absorbing the classical principles of garden design, and in France, where he honed his skills and developed his own unique aesthetic.  Crucially, he worked for the renowned landscape architect, Jean-Claude Forestier, in Paris, from 1966 to 1971, an experience that solidified his understanding of contemporary design trends and provided invaluable mentorship. 

Suarez’s professional career truly took off in the late 1970s and early 1980s. In 1978, he accepted the prestigious position of Chief Landscape Architect for the City of Paris, a role he held until 1989.  This tenure was extraordinarily productive. He spearheaded the redesign of numerous Parisian parks and gardens, including the Bois de Boulogne, a vast expanse of green space on the city’s western edge, and the Jardin Albert Kahn, a meticulously planned and restored garden showcasing a range of horticultural styles.  His work in Paris was characterized by a commitment to integrating contemporary design with the historical character of the sites, often incorporating sculptures and water features to create dynamic and engaging spaces.  He employed a significant team, overseeing approximately 60 staff members during his time in Paris.

Beyond Paris, Suarez's influence extended globally. He undertook commissions in countries as diverse as Spain (the Parque del Oeste in Madrid, completed in 1986), Portugal (the Parque das Nações in Lisbon, designed for the Expo '98), and Japan (the redesign of the Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden in Tokyo, a project completed in 1994), demonstrating a remarkable adaptability to different cultural contexts and climates.  He was particularly celebrated for his work in Spain, where he created numerous public parks and gardens that revitalized urban spaces and provided vital green lungs for cities like Seville and Valencia. 

In 1994, Suarez established his own design firm, Diego Suarez Landscape Architects, based in Barcelona, Spain. He continued to work on large-scale projects throughout Europe and Latin America until his retirement in 2008.  Throughout his career, Suarez received numerous awards and accolades, including the European Prize for Architectural Excellence in 1993 and the Spanish National Architecture Prize in 1999.  Diego Suarez passed away on 18 January 2018 in Barcelona, leaving behind a legacy of stunning and thoughtfully designed landscapes that continue to shape the urban and rural environments of countless cities and regions.

title: Joey Jordison
text:
Joseph James “Joey” Jordison was born on June 18, 1974, in Derry, Pennsylvania, to parents, Joseph and Mary Jordison. His childhood was marked by a difficult upbringing, frequently moving due to his father’s struggles with alcohol and gambling addiction. He spent significant periods living with his maternal grandmother, Helen, in the small town of Donegal, Pennsylvania, a rural area deeply rooted in Irish heritage. This isolation and a sense of being an outsider shaped his early personality, fostering a fierce independence and a drive to prove himself. He began drumming at the age of eight, initially learning on a makeshift kit constructed from buckets and pots and pans, a passion ignited by listening to bands like Metallica and Slayer. He quickly displayed a natural talent, teaching himself to play bass guitar and eventually mastering the drums, guitar, and vocals. 

Jordison’s musical journey began in the late 1980s with local bands in Pennsylvania. In 1989, he formed The Promise, a hardcore punk band that gained a local following.  He then joined the band “The Exes” in 1991, experiencing a brief stint in the Pittsburgh hardcore scene.  It was during this time that he honed his aggressive drumming style, a key element of his future success.  The Exes disbanded in 1993, and Jordison’s trajectory shifted dramatically when he relocated to Los Angeles, California, in 1994. 

His arrival in Los Angeles coincided with the burgeoning death metal scene. He quickly caught the attention of Hatebreed, a band founded by Jamey Jasta, and joined them in 1996.  Hatebreed’s breakthrough came in 1997 with their self-titled debut album, propelling them to national recognition and solidifying Jordison’s reputation as one of the most technically proficient and energetic drummers in the genre.  The band continued to release critically acclaimed albums – *Roots of a Ruin* (1998), *Suffocation* (2001), and *The Fallout* (2003) – establishing themselves as a cornerstone of the New Jersey hardcore movement. 

In 2002, Jordison’s explosive energy and unparalleled drumming skills led him to join Slipknot, a band he’d been a fan of since their early demos. He was officially brought into the group in 2003, replacing Paul Gray, who tragically passed away. Jordison’s addition was pivotal to Slipknot's sound, injecting a raw, chaotic intensity that defined their signature style. The band’s debut album, *Slipknot* (2004), went on to become a global phenomenon, reaching multi-platinum status and cementing Slipknot’s position as one of the biggest bands in the world. Subsequent albums – *Vol. 2: Session Recordings* (2006), *All Hope Is Gone* (2008), *Double Trouble* (2010), *We Are Not Your Kind* (2014), and *The End, So Far* (2019) – continued to push boundaries and maintain the band's commercial success, with *All Hope Is Gone* achieving Diamond certification by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA).  Throughout his tenure with Slipknot, Jordison was known for his intensely physical performances, often incorporating elaborate stage antics and showcasing his incredible speed and power. 

Beyond his work with Slipknot, Jordison pursued numerous side projects. He formed the metalcore band Demonic Resurrection in 2006, releasing their self-titled debut in 2007. He also collaborated with numerous artists, including Corey Taylor of Slipknot and Rob Zombie, and participated in various compilations and tribute albums.  He was a frequent touring musician, playing hundreds of shows annually with both Slipknot and his other bands. 

Sadly, Jordison’s life was marked by personal struggles. In 2015, he was diagnosed with ruptured axial ligaments in his neck, requiring surgery.  The surgery was unsuccessful, leading to a cascade of health issues, including a severe case of Lyme disease, which he attributed to a tick bite. He battled depression and substance abuse, publicly acknowledging his struggles in the years leading up to his death. 

On July 26, 2021, Joey Jordison passed away at the age of 46 in Orlando, Florida, due to acute liver inflammation, a consequence of his long-term substance abuse. His death was a profound loss to the metal community, and he is remembered as one of the most influential and undeniably energetic drummers in heavy metal history. He is survived by his wife, Kaylee VanderMeer, and his three children: Jordy, Journey, and Ever.

title: Daniel Alexander Cameron
text:
Daniel Alexander Cameron, often referred to as Dan Cameron, was a prominent American journalist, political commentator, and television personality, known for his sharp wit, conservative viewpoints, and extensive coverage of political events. Born on June 24, 1965, in Washington, D.C., his early life was steeped in a political environment. His father, Daniel Cameron Sr., was a Republican Congressman representing Maryland’s 3rd congressional district from 1981 to 1993, and his mother, Patricia (née DePrez), was a former White House social secretary during the Nixon administration. This lineage instilled in him a deep understanding of the American political landscape from a very young age.

Cameron’s formal education began at St. Albans School, a prestigious preparatory school in Bethesda, Maryland, where he excelled academically and participated in debate, honing his skills in argumentation and persuasive communication. He continued his education at Yale University, graduating in 1987 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science. During his time at Yale, he was an active member of the college’s newspaper, the *Yale Daily News*, gaining valuable experience in reporting and journalism.

Following graduation, Cameron embarked on his career in journalism, initially working as a reporter for *The Washington Star* newspaper in 1988. He quickly moved up the ranks, becoming an assistant city editor in 1991 and then a deputy city editor in 1993. This period provided him with a robust understanding of Washington D.C.’s political machinery and the daily operations of a major newspaper. He moved to *The Washington Times* in 1995, where he served as a political reporter and columnist, further solidifying his reputation as a conservative voice in the media. 

A pivotal moment in Cameron’s career arrived in 1997 when he joined Fox News Channel. He quickly became a key figure on the network, initially as a political analyst and later as the host of *The Big Issue* from 2001 to 2009. *The Big Issue* became a flagship program for Fox News, known for its in-depth interviews with political figures and its analysis of current events. During this time, Cameron interviewed numerous prominent individuals, including Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush, Vice Presidents Dick Cheney and Joe Biden, and countless members of Congress. He also conducted extensive interviews with foreign leaders, covering events in countries like Iraq, Afghanistan, and Iran. 

Beyond *The Big Issue*, Cameron contributed to various Fox News programs, including *Special Report with Bret Baier* and *Fox News Sunday*. He consistently provided insightful commentary and analysis on political developments, often offering a conservative perspective.  In 2009, he moved to CNN as a political commentator, where he continued to offer his opinions and analysis on a wide range of political topics. 

In 2018, Cameron joined SiriusXM, hosting the daily political program *The Dan Show*.  This allowed him to further expand his reach and engage directly with his audience. Throughout his career, Cameron has authored several books, including “The Big Issue: How the Democrats Seized the Presidency” (2003), a critical examination of the 2000 election, and “The Plot Against America” (2018), which explored the historical parallels between the rise of fascism in Europe and the political climate in the United States.

Later in life, Cameron remained active in the media landscape, continuing his work on SiriusXM and contributing to various online platforms. He relocated to San Antonio, Texas, in 2023, seeking a change of pace and a closer connection to his family. Daniel Alexander Cameron passed away on August 28, 2023, at the age of 58, following a battle with cancer. He is survived by his wife, Catherine, and their three children. His legacy as a respected journalist and political commentator will undoubtedly continue to resonate within the American media and political communities.

title: Ivan Perišić
text:
Ivan Perišić is a Croatian professional footballer widely regarded as one of the most versatile and reliable defenders in European football. Born on 24 February 1988 in Karlovac, Croatia, his journey from a local youth player to a seasoned international has been marked by consistent performance, tactical adaptability, and a quiet, professional demeanor. Perišić’s career trajectory reflects a dedication to the game and a willingness to embrace diverse roles on the pitch.

His early footballing development began at NK Karlovac, a club he joined in 1994, the same year he was born. He progressed through their youth ranks, demonstrating a natural aptitude for the sport. At the age of 16, in 2004, Perišić signed his first professional contract with NK Istra 1961, a club based in Pula, located on the Istrian peninsula. He spent three seasons with Istra, primarily playing as a left-back, contributing 31 appearances and scoring 3 goals across those years.  His time at Istra provided a crucial foundation for his future development, allowing him to gain valuable experience in the Croatian Prva Liga (the top tier of Croatian football).

In July 2007, Perišić made a significant step in his career, transferring to Dinamo Zagreb, Croatia’s dominant force in domestic football. This move marked a transition into a club renowned for its youth development and rigorous training. Initially, he was deployed as a left-back, but his versatility quickly became apparent.  During his seven years with Dinamo Zagreb (2007-2014), Perišić played a remarkable 326 competitive matches, scoring 24 goals and winning numerous titles, including the Croatian الدوري (1x), the Croatian Cup (3x), and the Croatian Super Cup (2x). Notably, in the 2012-2013 season, he was instrumental in Dinamo’s league triumph, appearing in 31 matches and contributing significantly to their defensive solidity.

Following his successful stint at Dinamo Zagreb, Perišić embarked on a series of moves across Europe, seeking new challenges and opportunities. In August 2014, he joined Sporting Lisbon in Portugal, where he spent two seasons, playing 64 matches and scoring 6 goals. He then moved to VfB Stuttgart in Germany in July 2016, appearing in 37 Bundesliga games and establishing himself as a dependable defender.  His time in Germany was cut short in January 2018 when he joined Tottenham Hotspur in the English Premier League.  Although he struggled to establish a consistent starting role at Spurs, he made 16 appearances, demonstrating his ability to compete at the highest level of European football.

In August 2018, Perišić returned to Croatia to join his former club, Dinamo Zagreb, on a free transfer. He spent another two seasons there, contributing to their 2018-2019 Croatian Cup victory.  In June 2020, he signed for Fiorentina in Italy, where he played for two seasons, accumulating 48 appearances and scoring 3 goals. Most recently, in August 2021, he joined Atalanta BC in Italy’s Serie A, where he continues to play as of November 2023. 

Perišić’s international career with Croatia began in 2007. He earned his first cap on 10 September 2007 against Russia. He has since become a mainstay in the Croatian national team, representing his country in numerous major tournaments. He was part of the Croatian squad that reached the final of Euro 2020 (delayed to 2021), playing in all of their group stage matches and several knockout rounds.  He earned his 100th international cap for Croatia in September 2023, solidifying his position as a national hero.  As of today, November 2, 2023, he has played 126 international matches, scoring 8 goals.  

Beyond his footballing achievements, Perišić is known for his quiet personality and dedication to his craft. He’s consistently demonstrated a commitment to fitness and tactical awareness, making him a valuable asset to any team he joins.  His career represents a testament to hard work, adaptability, and a genuine love for the game of football.

title: Muhammad Qutb
text:
Muhammad Qutb, born on November 14, 1906, in Cairo, Egypt, was a prominent and controversial Islamic scholar, intellectual, and activist whose ideas profoundly influenced the Muslim Brotherhood and, ultimately, the Jama’at al-Islami. His life, spanning nearly six decades, was marked by a passionate engagement with Islamic thought, a critique of Western colonialism and modernity, and a fervent belief in the necessity of a revolutionary Islamic revival. His trajectory, though initially focused on scholarly pursuits, took a dramatically ideological turn, culminating in his execution in 1966.

Qutb’s early life was steeped in religious learning. His father, Abdullah Qutb, a respected jurist and scholar of the Hanafi school of Islamic law, instilled in him a deep reverence for the Quran and traditional Islamic teachings. He received his primary education at the Dar al-Ulum al-Qahira, a prestigious Islamic school in Cairo, graduating in 1929 with a degree in Sharia (Islamic law).  He then pursued further studies at the Faculty of Theology at al-Azhar University, the oldest and most influential Islamic university in the world, earning his doctorate in 1932 with a dissertation on the concept of "Ihtiyat" – precautionary measures in Islamic jurisprudence.  This period solidified his understanding of Islamic law and philosophy, but also exposed him to the perceived shortcomings of traditional Islamic scholarship, particularly its reliance on secondary sources and its lack of engagement with contemporary social and political realities. 

In 1937, Qutb traveled to the United States on a scholarship to study for a Master's degree in Theology at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. This experience proved transformative. He became acutely aware of the profound impact of Western colonialism on the Muslim world, witnessing the exploitation and cultural destruction it wrought.  He observed the stark contrast between the perceived moral bankruptcy of Western societies and the purported virtues of traditional Islamic values.  He began to develop his distinctive interpretation of Islam, rooted in a radical reading of the Quran and a rejection of what he considered to be its historical deviations. He also became increasingly critical of secular nationalism, seeing it as a betrayal of Islamic principles.

Upon returning to Egypt in 1940, Qutb joined the Muslim Brotherhood, initially as a translator and editor for their publications. However, he quickly rose to prominence within the organization, largely due to his prolific writing and his ability to articulate a compelling vision of Islamic renewal.  He authored numerous influential pamphlets, essays, and books, including *Al-Milhama al-Islamiyya* (The Islamic Struggle, 1941), a seminal work that outlined his interpretation of Islamic history as a series of struggles between believers and enemies of Islam, and *Al-Jami’ al-Islami* (The Islamic Movement, 1942), which advocated for a global Islamic state governed by Islamic law.  His writings gained immense popularity, attracting a devoted following amongst Egyptian youth and intellectuals.

Qutb’s radicalization intensified in the late 1940s and early 1950s. He began to interpret the Quranic concept of "al-nahda" – the awakening – not simply as a call to religious reform, but as a call to a revolutionary transformation of society based on Islamic principles. He argued for the necessity of a “pure” Islamic state, rejecting any compromise with secularism or Western influence.  His increasingly strident criticism of the Egyptian government, which he viewed as corrupt and subservient to Western powers, led to his arrest in 1954. He spent nearly two years in prison, during which time he continued to write and develop his ideas, further solidifying his revolutionary stance. 

Following his release in 1956, Qutb became increasingly isolated and disillusioned. He formed his own independent Islamic movement, Jama’at al-Islami, which advocated for a more radical approach to Islamic governance.  In 1966, he was arrested again and, along with seventy-seven other Jama’at leaders, was summarily executed by President Gamal Abdel Nasser’s regime.  His death, a controversial event that sparked international condemnation, cemented his status as a martyr and a symbol of Islamic resistance to Western imperialism and secularism. 

Despite his tragically short life, Muhammad Qutb’s ideas continue to exert a powerful influence on Islamic movements around the world, particularly in the Middle East, shaping interpretations of Islamic law, politics, and social reform.  His legacy remains deeply debated, with some viewing him as a visionary reformer and others as a dangerous extremist.

title: Shin Jea-hwan
text:
Shin Jea-hwan (신재환), born Kim Jeong-hwan (김정환) on December 18, 1949, in the small coastal town of Wando, Jeju Island, South Korea, rose to become one of the most iconic and beloved figures in the history of Korean trot music. His life, marked by hardship, artistic dedication, and a remarkable comeback, is a testament to perseverance and the enduring power of soulful music. His early life on Jeju Island profoundly shaped his musical identity, steeped in the island’s unique blend of traditional Korean folk music, blues, and American country influences. Jeju, known as the “Island of the Gods,” offered a landscape of dramatic volcanic scenery and a strong maritime culture, which subtly infused Shin’s melancholic and deeply personal songs. 

Following the Korean War, his family moved to Seoul in 1957, seeking better opportunities. His father, a fisherman, struggled to find work, and the family faced considerable financial difficulties.  Shin’s musical journey began modestly, singing in local pubs and restaurants in the early 1970s, honing his distinctive baritone voice and developing his signature style – a blend of raw emotion, bluesy phrasing, and a subtle, almost mournful delivery. He initially performed under the name “Kim Jeong-hwan,” but adopted the stage name Shin Jea-hwan in 1974, a name that resonated with his audience and became inextricably linked to his music. 

Shin Jea-hwan’s breakthrough came in 1976 with the release of his debut album, "Lonely Night" (외로운 밤), produced by renowned music producer Park Joon-sun. The album, featuring the track “Lonely Night,” achieved immediate success, topping the charts and establishing him as a major force in the burgeoning trot scene. Trot, a genre blending Korean folk music with Western influences like jazz and blues, was experiencing a resurgence in popularity during the 1970s, and Shin Jea-hwan quickly became its leading figure.  Subsequent albums, including “Tears of a Lonely Man” (외로운 남자의 눈물) in 1978 and "My Heart's Sorrow" (마음의 상처) in 1980, solidified his reputation for emotionally resonant ballads. 

Throughout the 1980s, Shin Jea-hwan dominated the Korean music industry. He released a prolific number of albums, consistently achieving platinum sales and selling over 15 million records throughout his career.  He became known for his meticulously crafted live performances, often featuring elaborate stage sets and incorporating elements of traditional Korean dance. His signature song, "Lonely Night," remains arguably his most recognizable work, frequently cited as the quintessential trot ballad.  He held the record for the most number-one hits on the Korean music charts for a remarkable 18 years, a record that stood until 2004. 

However, Shin’s career took a devastating turn in 1988.  He was arrested and convicted of tax evasion, a crime that stemmed from a complex financial scheme involving a brokerage firm. He was sentenced to five years in prison, effectively ending his music career. He served nearly three years at the Seoul Penitentiary, a period he described as incredibly difficult and isolating. 

Following his release in 1991, Shin Jea-hwan faced immense public scrutiny and struggled to regain his former status.  He attempted a comeback in 1993 with the album “Prisoner’s Tears” (수감자의 눈물), but it was met with lukewarm reception.  Despite the initial disappointment, Shin remained dedicated to his music, continuing to perform occasionally and write songs in private. 

In 2004, at the age of 55, Shin Jea-hwan staged an incredible comeback with the release of “The Return” (돌아와), an album that was a massive commercial and critical success. The album, featuring the title track "The Return," topped the charts and generated widespread media attention.  This triumphant return marked a significant moment in Korean music history, demonstrating the enduring appeal of Shin Jea-hwan’s music and his unwavering commitment to his art.  He continued to release albums and perform live shows until his death on June 2, 2012, in Seoul, at the age of 62, from complications related to a stroke. Shin Jea-hwan’s legacy as a pioneer of trot music and a symbol of resilience continues to inspire generations of Korean musicians and fans.

title: Gemma Arterton
text:
Gemma Arterton, born Gemma Christina Arterton on June 2, 1986, in Addington, Croydon, Surrey, England, is a highly successful and versatile British actress known for her captivating performances across film and theatre. Her journey began with a childhood immersed in the performing arts, a path largely influenced by her parents – her father, John Arterton, a former soldier, and her mother, Anne Arterton, a stage manager. She spent her early years in various locations, including a brief stint in Australia with her family, before returning to England to attend the Hammond School, a prestigious boarding school in Chesham, Buckinghamshire, where she excelled in drama. Arterton’s dedication to acting was solidified during her time at the Brit School in London from 1999 to 2003, a training ground for numerous musical theatre and pop music stars, including Adele, Amy Winehouse, and Leona Lewis. 

Arterton's professional career began with a small role in the 2004 film *Closer*, directed by Mark Cousins, a debut that quickly garnered attention. However, her breakthrough came in 2006 with her portrayal of the courageous and resourceful Lyra Belacqua in *Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time*, directed by Rob Schneider. The film, a massive global box office success, grossing over $343 million worldwide, catapulted her into international stardom and cemented her status as a leading action heroine. This role showcased her physicality and ability to portray a strong, independent character, skills she would continue to utilize throughout her career.

Following *Prince of Persia*, Arterton continued to build a diverse filmography, tackling a range of genres and roles. In 2008, she starred in *Quantum of Solace*, the second installment of the James Bond series, playing Eve Moneypenny, a complex and intelligent intelligence operative. This marked a significant step up in terms of prestige and exposure, and she quickly became a regular face in high-profile action films.  She appeared in *Midsummer Night’s Dream* (2010), directed by Mike Newmark, a vibrant and imaginative adaptation of Shakespeare’s classic, earning her a nomination for the Best Actress Award at the British Independent Film Awards. 

Arterton’s commitment to theatre remained a significant part of her artistic life. She made her West End debut in 2008 in *Red* at the Gate Theatre, London, and later starred in *Romeo and Juliet* at Shakespeare's Globe in 2012, a production directed by Gary Oldman. This marked a return to her theatrical roots and demonstrated her dedication to classical storytelling.  In 2014, she returned to the stage, playing the role of Lady Macbeth in a critically acclaimed production of *Macbeth* at the Old Vic Theatre in London.

Beyond action and period dramas, Arterton has demonstrated her versatility with roles in films such as *Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy* (2011), a critically lauded espionage thriller directed by Steven Spielberg, where she portrayed Susan Hill, a vital member of British intelligence; *Suffragette* (2015), a historical drama depicting the early women's suffrage movement in Britain, for which she received widespread praise; and *The Rhythm Section* (2020), a stylish action thriller.  Her performance as Sofie Duvall in *The Rhythm Section* was particularly noted for its intensity and physicality. 

In 2019, Arterton made her directorial debut with *The Surface*, a short horror film. She has also continued to work steadily in film, appearing in *Funny Woman* (2022) and *Portraits* (2023).  

Arterton's personal life is relatively private. She began dating actor Richard Madden in 2010 and they married in a private ceremony in Italy on June 26, 2015, and welcomed their first child, daughter Elsie Viola Madden, on February 23, 2017.  They welcomed their second child, son River Madden, on December 17, 2020.  Despite her global fame, Gemma Arterton remains dedicated to her craft and consistently seeks challenging and diverse roles, solidifying her position as one of Britain’s most respected and accomplished actresses.  She currently resides with her family in Surrey.

title: Jeremy Corbyn
text:
Jeremy Corbyn’s life and career have been inextricably linked to the Labour Party and, more profoundly, to the British peace movement. Born on May 24, 1946, in Chippenham, Wiltshire, to a Jewish family, his early life was shaped by a strong sense of social justice and a growing awareness of international conflicts. His father, Stanley Corbyn, was a schoolteacher and a staunch pacifist, a philosophy that profoundly influenced young Jeremy. He attended King’s College School in Canterbury from 1958 to 1963, followed by a year at the University of Manchester Institute of Technology studying engineering, though he left without completing a degree.

Corbyn’s political awakening began in the late 1960s, joining the Hackney Young Socialist movement in London. This marked his entry into the Labour Party, where he quickly rose through the ranks. He became involved with the Greater East London Trades Council in 1970, a position he held for nearly 25 years, becoming General Secretary in 1989. This role provided him with extensive experience in working with trade unions and grassroots activism, particularly within the transport sector. During this time, he was a key figure in organising strikes and campaigns against privatisation, most notably the 1989-90 London Dock Strike, a pivotal moment in the anti-privatisation movement. He played a significant role in the leadership of the National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers (RMT) from 1984 to 1998, leading campaigns against the closure of the Docklands Light Railway and fighting for the rights of rail workers.

Corbyn’s political career within the Labour Party began in 1983 when he was elected as the MP for Islington North, a constituency with a long history of socialist representation. He has held this seat continuously since, making him the longest-serving MP currently in the House of Commons. His early years in Parliament were marked by a focus on social justice issues, particularly housing and poverty. He served as Shadow Secretary of State for Employment from 1987 to 1992 and Shadow Secretary of State for Health from 1992 to 1997.  He gained a reputation as a tenacious and uncompromising advocate for the working class.

In 2003, Corbyn became the Shadow Foreign Secretary under Tony Blair. While holding this position, he publicly opposed the 2003 invasion of Iraq, a stance that would later define his political trajectory. He famously delivered a scathing critique of the war in the House of Commons on February 16, 2003, arguing that it was based on “misinformation and deceit.” This dissent led to him being deselected as the Labour candidate for Islington North in the 2005 general election, a deeply painful experience for him.

Following his deselection, Corbyn established the Campaign Group, a pressure group advocating for a new socialist vision within the Labour Party. He remained an independent MP, continuing to champion peace and international solidarity. In 2015, he was unexpectedly elected as Leader of the Labour Party, defeating Ed Miliband in a dramatic leadership contest. 

As Leader, Corbyn oversaw a significant shift in the party’s platform, embracing policies advocating for greater investment in public services, increased trade union rights, and a more critical stance on foreign policy. He spearheaded campaigns against arms sales, supported the Scottish independence movement, and championed the plight of Palestinian refugees. However, his leadership was also marked by controversy, including accusations of antisemitism within the party, which he faced criticism for not adequately addressing.  In April 2019, following a heavy defeat in the general election, Corbyn announced his resignation as Labour leader on December 31, 2019.  He remains an MP for Islington North and continues to be a prominent voice in the Labour Party and the wider political landscape, advocating for peace and social justice.

title: Nuh Omar
text:
Nuh Omar, born in 1934 in the rural village of Al-Jabal, in the Al-Sharqiyah Governorate of Saudi Arabia, was a pioneering figure in the field of Saudi Arabian aviation and a key contributor to the nation’s burgeoning aerospace industry. His life, marked by a relentless pursuit of knowledge and a dedication to national development, began in a modest setting, far removed from the high-tech world he would eventually shape.  His father, Abdullah bin Hamad Al-Thani, was a farmer, and his mother, Fatima bint Salem Al-Malki, instilled in him a strong sense of family and community values.  Growing up in Al-Jabal, a region known for its date palm plantations and traditional Bedouin culture, Nuh developed a practical understanding of mechanics and an early fascination with machines, likely fueled by observing the rudimentary tools and equipment used in agricultural life. 

In 1952, at the age of 18, Nuh Omar left Al-Jabal to pursue his education in the United States, a significant step for a young man from a rural village. He enrolled at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Aeronautical Engineering in 1956. This marked a pivotal moment, exposing him to cutting-edge technologies and theoretical knowledge that would become the foundation of his future career.  During his time at MIT, he excelled in aerodynamics and propulsion systems, demonstrating an aptitude for complex calculations and a meticulous approach to problem-solving.  He also actively participated in the MIT Aeronautical Society, further broadening his network and understanding of the aerospace field. 

Returning to Saudi Arabia in 1956, Omar joined the Royal Saudi Air Force (RSAF), an institution then undergoing rapid modernization. Initially, he was assigned to the Air Force’s Maintenance Department, a crucial role in ensuring the operational readiness of the burgeoning fleet of aircraft. However, his ambition quickly surpassed routine maintenance.  In 1961, he was selected to participate in the first Saudi Arabian delegation to the United States, traveling to Cleveland, Ohio, to study the design and manufacturing of the Boeing 707, a revolutionary jet airliner. This was a watershed moment, solidifying his understanding of commercial aviation and sparking a desire to contribute to the development of Saudi Arabia’s own aviation capabilities. 

Over the next two decades, Nuh Omar became instrumental in establishing Saudi Arabia’s aerospace industry. He was appointed as the Director of the Aircraft Maintenance Department at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh in 1968, a position he held until 1976.  During this time, he oversaw the establishment of the Kingdom’s first aircraft maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) facility, known as the Saudi Aerospace Industrial Complex (SAIC), which officially opened in 1977.  This complex, located in Riyadh, represented a monumental achievement – a completely indigenous capability for servicing and repairing a wide range of aircraft, including Boeing 707s, 737s, and Airbus A300s.  The initial investment was approximately $35 million, and the facility employed over 1,000 people within its first five years. 

Omar’s influence extended beyond the SAIC. He played a vital role in negotiating contracts with international aircraft manufacturers, including Boeing and Airbus, securing vital partnerships and technology transfer agreements. He was also deeply involved in the training of Saudi engineers and technicians, ensuring a skilled workforce to support the growing industry.  In 1976, he was appointed as the General Manager of the Saudi Arabian Airlines Corporation (Saudia), a position he held until his retirement in 1992.  During his tenure, Saudia experienced significant growth, expanding its route network and modernizing its fleet, adding aircraft such as the Boeing 747 and the Airbus A310. 

Throughout his career, Nuh Omar received numerous accolades, including the King Abdulaziz Humanitarian Prize for Distinguished Service in 1984. He remained an active member of the Royal Commission for the Development of Jubail Industrial City, contributing to the diversification of the Saudi economy.  Nuh Omar passed away in Riyadh on November 23, 2018, at the age of 84. His legacy as a visionary leader and a cornerstone of Saudi Arabia’s aviation industry continues to inspire, and the SAIC, now a globally recognized MRO provider, stands as a testament to his foresight and dedication.

title: Jeff Long (athletic director)
text:
Jeffrey “Jeff” Long was born on December 28, 1965, in Toledo, Ohio, the son of Robert and Mary Long. His upbringing in a middle-class family instilled in him a strong work ethic and a deep appreciation for sports, particularly football, which became a defining element of his life. He attended Toledo Central Catholic High School, a Catholic school known for its strong athletic programs, where he excelled as a linebacker and earned All-Ohio honors in 1984. This early success fueled his ambition to pursue a career in collegiate athletics, a path he initially considered through a degree in marketing. He enrolled at Bowling Green State University in 1984, intending to study marketing, but quickly shifted his focus to sports administration, realizing his passion lay in the behind-the-scenes operations that supported athletic programs.

Long began his professional career in 1988 as an administrative assistant for the athletic department at Bowling Green, a position he held for three years. This initial role provided invaluable experience, allowing him to learn the intricacies of budgeting, compliance, and personnel management within a college athletic environment. In 1991, he transitioned to Youngstown State University, where he served as an assistant athletic director for six years, overseeing various operational aspects of the university’s athletics program.  During this time, he gained significant experience in fundraising, facilities management, and student-athlete welfare. 

His trajectory accelerated dramatically in 1997 when he accepted the role of Deputy Athletic Director at the University of Iowa. This marked a pivotal moment in his career, placing him within the Big Ten Conference – a highly competitive landscape that demanded strategic thinking and strong leadership.  Under the guidance of Athletic Director Gary Gavrus, Long quickly proved himself a capable and diligent administrator, taking on increasing responsibilities including overseeing the department's budget, compliance, and external relations. 

In 2000, Long was promoted to Athletic Director at Iowa, succeeding Gavrus. His tenure at Iowa was marked by significant growth and controversy. He oversaw a period of substantial investment in athletic facilities, including the construction of Kinnick Stadium’s west side expansion in 2003, which increased seating capacity by over 6,000 and boosted revenue.  He also spearheaded the renovation of Carver-Hawkeye Arena, home to the Iowa men's basketball team, completed in 2009.  During his leadership, the Hawkeyes experienced considerable success across multiple sports. The football program consistently achieved bowl eligibility, culminating in a College Football Playoff appearance in 2015 – Iowa’s first appearance in the playoff since 1998.  The men’s basketball team also reached the NCAA Tournament multiple times, and the women’s gymnastics program achieved national prominence.  Overall, during his 17 years at Iowa, the athletic department generated over $147 million in revenue during the 2015-16 academic year. 

However, Long’s time at Iowa was not without challenges. In 2011, he faced intense scrutiny and criticism after allegations surfaced regarding the handling of a former football player’s academic misconduct case.  The player, James Woody, had been accused of cheating on coursework, and Long’s decision to initially allow Woody to play football despite the allegations sparked significant backlash and ultimately led to Woody’s suspension and subsequent dismissal.  This incident significantly damaged his reputation and prompted a comprehensive review of the university's athletic compliance procedures. 

In 2017, Long accepted the position of Athletic Director at Clemson University, succeeding Dan Radovich.  At Clemson, he continued his focus on strategic investments in facilities and technology, including the completion of the new IPTay Stadium in 2010 (though his tenure at Clemson began before that).  He also prioritized student-athlete development and academic success.  Under his leadership, Clemson’s athletic program experienced unprecedented success, particularly in football. The Clemson Tigers became a perennial national championship contender, winning three consecutive NCAA Division I FBS national championships from 2016 to 2018, a feat unmatched in modern college football.  His tenure concluded in June 2023, after a tumultuous period involving allegations of misconduct and a subsequent investigation.  He left Clemson amid an ongoing internal review and a legal battle with the university.  

As of late 2023, Long resides in Houston, Texas, and is currently involved in consulting work within the athletic administration field.  He remains a prominent figure in collegiate athletics, though his legacy is now inextricably linked to both remarkable achievements and significant controversy.

title: Jackie Shroff
text:
Jackie Shroff, born Krishnam Raju Shroff on 23 August 1967, in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India, is an Indian actor, producer, and martial artist who has carved a distinctive path in Bollywood and beyond. His journey began far from the glitz and glamour of the film industry, rooted in a background of martial arts and a family steeped in the entertainment world. His father, Rajasheela Shroff, was a renowned stuntman and action choreographer, and his mother, Indra Banerjea, was a popular actress who appeared in numerous Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu films during the 1960s and 70s. This upbringing profoundly shaped his early life and introduced him to the world of cinema at a very young age.

Growing up in Mumbai, Jackie’s childhood was spent immersed in martial arts training. He began his training in Taekwondo at the age of six under the tutelage of Master Chen, a Taiwanese Taekwondo master. He later transitioned to Kalaripayattu, an ancient Indian martial art, and also studied Judo and Karate. This rigorous training instilled in him a discipline, physicality, and a remarkable ability to perform stunts – qualities that would become hallmarks of his career. He even earned the title of a black belt in Taekwondo. His father, Rajasheela, recognized his son's potential and began to involve him in film sets, initially as a background actor and eventually as a stunt double for various actors, including Amitabh Bachchan and Rajesh Khanna. 

Jackie's formal film debut came in 1983 with *Hero*, directed by Subhash Ghai. Although he didn’t have a significant role, he was credited as "Krish" in the film. However, his breakthrough arrived in 1989 with *Hera Pheri*, another Subhash Ghai production.  In this film, he played the role of ‘Kancha Singh,’ a menacing antagonist, and showcased his martial arts skills and intense screen presence. *Hera Pheri*, a box office success, solidified his position as a promising actor and established his signature style – a rugged, action-oriented persona. 

The 1990s saw a consistent stream of roles for Shroff, largely within the action and thriller genres, frequently directed by Subhash Ghai. Films like *Khalnayak* (1993), where he played the anti-hero ‘Ranjit,’ *Jo Bole Prabhat Chaye* (1995), *Ram Lakhan* (1992), and *Hero: Love Story of a Hero* (1995) showcased his versatility and cemented his popularity.  He was particularly noted for his ability to portray complex characters with a strong moral compass, often operating outside the conventional good and bad dichotomy.  *Khalnayak* earned him a Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor.  

Beyond Bollywood, Jackie gained recognition for his work in Tamil cinema. He made his Tamil debut in 1996 with *Ahnadu*, followed by *Karna* (1997) and *Pazhanji* (1999).  He continued to appear in Telugu films as well, including *Anji* (1999) and *Okka Chellelu* (2000).  He was known for his commitment to physically demanding roles, often undertaking elaborate fight sequences and stunts himself. 

Throughout his career, Shroff has worked with numerous prominent directors, including Yash Chopra, Karan Arjun, and Shirish Kunder. He’s appeared in over 70 films, with notable performances in *Baaghi* (2016), *Rani Maa* (2017), and *Prodnyudyog* (2023).  He has also ventured into production, establishing Jackie Shroff Productions in 2007, which has produced films like *Apor Sansar* (2010) and *Chya Lagna* (2016). 

In recent years, Shroff has increasingly focused on independent films and documentaries. He has been a vocal advocate for environmental conservation and has participated in several campaigns related to wildlife protection, notably supporting the efforts of the Wildlife Trust of India. He’s become a respected figure within the Indian film industry, admired for his dedication to his craft, his unconventional approach to acting, and his genuine passion for social causes. As of 2023, Jackie Shroff continues to act, produce, and advocate, demonstrating a sustained and impactful presence in the world of cinema and beyond.

title: Sami Shalom Chetrit
text:
Sami Shalom Chetrit (1927-2017) was a prominent Israeli businessman and philanthropist, widely recognized as one of the founding fathers of Israel’s real estate development industry. Born in Baghdad, Iraq, his life trajectory represents a remarkable story of immigration, entrepreneurial drive, and significant contribution to the economic growth of Israel. His journey began in the bustling, impoverished Al-Mansour district of Baghdad, a neighborhood predominantly populated by Sephardic Jewish immigrants from Spain and Portugal. His father, Shalom Chetrit, was a successful textile merchant, instilling in young Sami an early understanding of commerce and the value of hard work. Sami received his initial education in Baghdad, attending the Jewish elementary school of Al-Mansour, a crucial institution that fostered a sense of community and provided a foundation for his future endeavors. 

The political climate in Iraq steadily deteriorated in the late 1940s, with increasing anti-Jewish sentiment culminating in the 1948 Arab-Israeli War. Recognizing the instability and danger, Sami, his parents, and his siblings made the courageous decision to immigrate to Israel in 1949. They arrived in the newly declared State of Israel with limited resources, settling in the crowded and impoverished Florentine neighborhood of Jaffa. This experience deeply shaped his understanding of the challenges faced by new immigrants and fueled his ambition to create opportunities for others. 

Initially, Sami worked as a laborer, undertaking various manual jobs to support his family. He quickly demonstrated an innate business acumen, recognizing opportunities for small-scale trading and repair work.  In 1953, he established Chetrit Construction Company, starting with modest renovations and building projects. The company’s initial focus was on providing housing for incoming immigrants, a critical need in the rapidly expanding nation. This early work established a strong reputation for quality and reliability, laying the groundwork for future expansion. 

The 1960s witnessed a period of explosive growth in Israel, driven by immigration and a burgeoning economy. Chetrit Construction capitalized on this growth, diversifying its operations and expanding into larger-scale residential and commercial developments. A pivotal moment came in 1968 when he formed Chetrit Group, a holding company that encompassed Chetrit Construction and several other subsidiaries. This strategic move allowed for greater investment and control over a wider range of projects. 

Throughout the 1970s and 80s, Chetrit Group became a dominant force in Israeli real estate. The company’s projects included the iconic Azrieli Center in Tel Aviv (completed in 1981), a landmark skyscraper that became a symbol of Israeli ambition and architectural innovation.  The Azrieli Center was a particularly audacious undertaking, representing an initial investment of approximately $75 million and employing over 1,000 workers during its construction.  Chetrit Group also developed numerous other high-rise buildings across Israel, including projects in Jerusalem, Haifa, and Be’er Sheva.  By the late 1980s, the company’s portfolio encompassed over 60 million square feet of developed real estate, a testament to his strategic vision and execution. 

Beyond real estate, Chetrit also ventured into other sectors, including hotels and shopping centers. He was a pioneer in incorporating advanced building technologies and sustainable design principles into his projects, reflecting a forward-thinking approach to development.  Throughout his career, Sami consistently prioritized creating high-quality, mixed-use developments that integrated residential, commercial, and recreational spaces. 

In his later years, Sami Shalom Chetrit became a significant philanthropist, dedicating a substantial portion of his wealth to supporting education, healthcare, and cultural institutions. He established the Sami and Leah Chetrit Foundation, which has provided millions of dollars in grants to various charitable organizations across Israel. He was particularly passionate about supporting students from disadvantaged backgrounds and promoting access to higher education.  He passed away in Tel Aviv in 2017 at the age of 90, leaving behind a legacy as one of Israel’s most successful and influential entrepreneurs, and a deeply generous benefactor to the nation. His contributions fundamentally shaped the urban landscape of Israel and provided opportunities for countless individuals.

title: José Hernández Delgadillo
text:
José Hernández Delgadillo, a towering figure in Mexican and international boxing, was born on November 22, 1953, in Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico. His early life was steeped in the working-class environment of the city’s southern neighborhoods, a landscape where boxing served as both an escape and a potential path to a better future. His father, José Hernández, a former amateur boxer himself, instilled in him a love for the sport and initially trained him in the local *lucha libre* style, a precursor to modern boxing, emphasizing grappling and acrobatic maneuvers. Delgadillo began his amateur career at the age of 14, competing in the local *Liga Municipal de Boxeo* in Guadalajara. He quickly demonstrated a natural talent for the sport, characterized by his aggressive style, relentless pressure, and surprising punching power.
